questions.question: Q1. An arm structural design has a calculated Safety Factor ($SF$) of $0.82$. What mechanical behavior will occur if this drone attempts to fly?

answers.a: The arm will remain elastic but rotate slightly
answers.b: The arm will experience plastic yield deformation or fracture under load
answers.c: The arm will experience no change because 0.82 is close to 1.0
answers.d: The arm will become stiffer to resist the load

explanations.a: Incorrect — Elastic deformation only occurs when applied stress remains below yield strength (SF > 1.0).
explanations.b: Correct — Since SF < 1.0, the applied flexural stress exceeds the material's yield strength, resulting in permanent plastic deformation or mechanical fracture.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Any safety factor less than 1.0 indicates structural failure.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Materials cannot dynamically increase their innate stiffness (Young's Modulus) under load.

questions.question: Q2. Which material property dictates the flexural stiffness (resistance to bending deflection) of a drone's arm?

explanations.a: Incorrect — Yield strength defines the stress threshold for permanent damage, not the deflection stiffness.
explanations.b: Correct — Young's Modulus E represents the material's innate elastic stiffness (stress/strain ratio), which resists elastic bending deflection.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Density determines component weight, not bending resistance.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Specific heat capacity is a thermal storage constant.

questions.question: Q3. Why does a hollow rectangular tube section have a higher strength-to-weight ratio in bending compared to a solid rectangular rod of the same weight?

answers.a: Hollow sections have a higher material density
answers.b: Material is concentrated further from the neutral axis, maximizing the area moment of inertia ($I$) per unit mass
answers.c: Hollow sections experience zero shear force
answers.d: Hollow profiles have a lower Young's Modulus

explanations.a: Incorrect — Density is an innate material constant, independent of geometric section profile.
explanations.b: Correct — Flexural stress increases with distance from the neutral axis. Concentrating material at the outer flanges maximizes the moment of inertia I while removing low-stress core material, minimizing mass.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Hollow tubes still experience shear force loads.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Young's Modulus is a material property, not a shape parameter.

questions.question: Q4. If we double the wall thickness ($t$) of a hollow rectangular arm while keeping its outer dimensions ($b$ and $h$) constant, what is the effect on the area moment of inertia ($I$)?

answers.a: It decreases because the arm has less void space
answers.b: It increases, thereby lowering the maximum bending stress under a constant load
answers.c: It remains unchanged because the outer envelope dimensions are constant
answers.d: It drops to zero at the neutral plane

explanations.a: Incorrect — Adding material thickness increases structural moment of inertia, not decreases it.
explanations.b: Correct — Thickening the wall reduces the inner void area, which increases the area moment of inertia I. Since stress is inversely proportional to I, the maximum bending stress decreases.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Wall thickness alters the inner void boundary, modifying the cross-section inertia.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Moment of inertia is an integral property of the entire cross-section and does not drop to zero.

questions.question: Q5. During a stress test on a Nylon (PA6) arm with $350\text{ mm}$ length, the safety factor drops below 1.0. Why does Nylon behave so poorly compared to Aluminium 6061-T6 under identical thrust loads?

answers.b: Nylon has a much lower yield strength (50 MPa vs. 270 MPa) and lower stiffness (2 GPa vs. 69 GPa)
answers.c: Nylon has a higher area moment of inertia
answers.d: Nylon experiences higher bending moments for the same arm length

explanations.a: Incorrect — Nylon is actually lighter (density 1.14 g/cm^3) than Aluminium (2.7 g/cm^3), but is mechanically weaker.
explanations.b: Correct — Nylon's yield strength (50 MPa) is less than 20% of Aluminium's (270 MPa), and its low Young's Modulus (2 GPa) causes massive flexural deflection.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Moment of inertia depends on the geometric shape, not material choice.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Bending moment depends on load and arm length, which are identical in this comparison.

questions.question: Q6. In real-world drone operations, what is a primary limitation of using a purely static cantilever bending stress model for arm safety predictions?

answers.a: It ignores dynamic bending spikes from motor vibrations and gyroscopic maneuvering loads
answers.b: It assumes gravity does not act on the motor weight
answers.c: It overestimates the yield strength of the materials
answers.d: It cannot account for the length of the arm

explanations.a: Correct — Static models reflect stationary hover. Dynamic maneuvers (sudden pitches/rolls) and rotor vibrations can spike actual arm loading forces by 1.5x to 3x static estimates.
explanations.b: Incorrect — The static equation includes motor weight force (m * g).
explanations.c: Incorrect — Yield strength is a constant material property and is not modified by the stress model.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The cantilever equation explicitly incorporates arm length L.

questions.question: Q7. What is the consequence of an unbalanced Center of Gravity ($y_{\mathrm{CG}} > 10\text{ mm}$) along the longitudinal pitch axis during a live flight simulation?

answers.a: The battery pack cell capacity will drop by 20%
answers.b: The front motors must spin faster than the rear motors to maintain pitch trim, causing motor thermal runaway
answers.c: The propellers will automatically spin in reverse
answers.d: The drag coefficient of the body drops

explanations.a: Incorrect — CG imbalance is a mechanical force offset, it does not alter battery capacity.
explanations.b: Correct — If the drone is nose-heavy (y_cg > 10mm), the front motors must work harder to generate pitching counter-torque, drawing higher current and rapidly heating up.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Propellers do not spin in reverse to balance a drone.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Drag coefficient is unaffected by CG placement.

questions.question: Q8. According to Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, how does the beam's maximum tip deflection ($y_{\mathrm{max}}$) scale with the length of the arm ($L$)?

explanations.a: Incorrect — Deflection scales much faster than linear.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Deflection slope scales quadratically, but tip displacement scales higher.
explanations.c: Correct — According to deflection equations, tip deflection is $y_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{F \cdot L^3}{3 E I}$, which scales cubically with length.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Thrust scales quartically with propeller diameter, but beam deflection scales cubically with length.

questions.question: Q9. Why is a structural safety factor threshold of $SF \ge 2.0$ commonly enforced in commercial drone design guidelines?

answers.a: To account for material fatigue, manufacturing defects, and dynamic load amplification factors
answers.b: To ensure the drone is as heavy as possible to resist wind gusts
answers.c: To ensure the flight controller board remains cool
answers.d: To force the propellers to operate at maximum efficiency

explanations.a: Correct — Enforcement of SF >= 2.0 provides a 100% safety buffer to account for dynamic flight loads, structural fatigue over time, and imperfections in the material sheets.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Heavy drones require more hover power, reducing payload capacity and flight times.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Structural safety factors do not influence board electronics cooling.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Aerodynamic efficiency is independent of arm safety factor thresholds.

questions.question: Q10. How does the 'Rigid Body' assumption affect Center of Gravity calculations compared to real-world drone flights?

answers.a: It assumes components never change weight, which is incorrect as fuel burns
answers.b: It ignores flexible structural deflections (like battery strap sagging or arm flexing) which can dynamically shift the CG mid-flight
answers.c: It forces motors to draw 50% higher current
answers.d: It alters the gravitational acceleration constant

explanations.a: Incorrect — Drones use battery electrical power, which does not change weight during discharge (unlike gas-powered engines).
explanations.b: Correct — Real components are not perfectly rigid. Soft mounts, strap sags, and arm deflections shift component centroids under high-G maneuvers, dynamically displacing the CG.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Rigid assumptions do not scale electrical current draw directly.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Gravity g is a local constant.
